desc:
A string w is a supersequence of a string x if x can be obtained from w by deleting some characters (possibly none) without reordering the rest. Equivalently, x is a subsequence of w.

Given strings a and b, return the length of the shortest string that is a supersequence of both.

a = "abac", b = "cab"  ->  5   ("cabac" contains both)
a = "geek", b = "eke"  ->  5   ("geeke")
a = "abc",  b = "xyz"  ->  6
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Writing a and b one after the other always gives a valid answer of length a.length + b.length. When can you do better?
You save one character every time a character of a and a character of b can be written as the same character of the result. Which characters can be shared in this way?
The shared characters form a common subsequence of a and b (their relative order must be preserved in both strings). Share as many as possible: the answer is len(a) + len(b) - LCS(a, b).
editorial: Build a supersequence by merging a and b like a zip: at every step write a character that advances a, b, or both. Writing a character that advances both is only possible when the two next characters are equal. Every such shared step saves one character compared to plain concatenation. The characters that are shared, read in order, form a string that is a subsequence of a and of b.

Conversely, any common subsequence of length k can be turned into a supersequence of length len(a) + len(b) - k: write the pieces of a and b that lie between consecutive matched characters, then the matched character once. So the shortest supersequence has length len(a) + len(b) - L where L is the length of the longest common subsequence.
Compute L with the usual table, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 on a match and max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) otherwise, keeping only the previous row.
